meta.title: The Roof of the World: Mount Everest and Its Base Camps
meta.subtitle: Two camps, one summit, and the widening gap between elite mountaineering and mass commercial guiding

report_card.summary: Mount Everest is climbed from two base camps — Nepali South Base Camp and Tibetan North Base Camp — each staging a different route, national permitting regime, and climbing culture. Since Hillary and Norgay's 1953 first ascent, the mountain has moved from an expedition-era physiological frontier to a commercial guiding market, and that shift has repeatedly collided with the mountain's fixed hazards: the Khumbu Icefall, the death zone above 8,000 m, and a warming glacier. The result is a recurring pattern — 1996, 2014, 2015, 2019 — in which rising climber volume and thin regulation turn known hazards into mass-casualty events, while the Sherpa community absorbs the largest share of the risk.

story.title: Two Doors to the Roof of the World
story.narration: Every Everest attempt begins at one of two base camps: South Base Camp in Nepal at 5,364 m, or North Base Camp in Tibet at 5,150 m. The two sides differ in access, hazard profile, and administering government, but converge on the same 8,849 m summit.

story.title: The Nepali Approach and the Icefall Doctors
story.narration: From South Base Camp, climbers face the Khumbu Icefall almost immediately — a shifting field of house-sized ice seracs crossed dozens of times per expedition on ladders and ropes maintained by the Icefall Doctors, a dedicated Sherpa team. The trek in itself, from Lukla's airstrip, already sets the Nepali side apart from the vehicle-accessible north.

story.title: 1953: Hillary and Norgay Reach the Summit
story.narration: On 29 May 1953, Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reach the summit via the South Col route, part of John Hunt's British expedition. It is the foundational event of Everest mountaineering — the moment the mountain moves from an unclimbed problem to a proven, still-lethal objective.

story.title: Mallory's Unanswered Question
story.narration: Nearly three decades earlier, George Mallory and Andrew Irvine disappeared high on the North Ridge in 1924, leaving open whether they summited before dying. Mallory's body was found in 1999; Irvine's has never been located, and the question outlives both the men and the 1953 ascent that settled the matter for the record books.

story.title: Messner and Habeler Break the Oxygen Barrier
story.narration: In 1978, Reinhold Messner and Peter Habeler summit without supplemental oxygen, a feat many mountaineers of the era considered physiologically impossible above 8,000 m. Their ascent reframes the upper limits of unassisted human performance inside the death zone.

story.title: 1996: A Storm Catches the Commercial Era
story.narration: A rogue storm traps multiple guided groups near the summit on 10–11 May 1996, killing eight climbers in a single day, including Adventure Consultants founder Rob Hall and Mountain Madness founder Scott Fischer. Jon Krakauer survives and chronicles it in "Into Thin Air," cementing the disaster as the defining cautionary tale about commercial climbing volume.

story.title: Sherpa Labor Bears the Weight
story.narration: On 18 April 2014, an avalanche in the Khumbu Icefall kills sixteen Nepali guides and porters, triggering a labor action that shuts down that season's climbing. The disaster exposes how disproportionately the Sherpa community — the Icefall Doctors, the rope-fixers, record-holder Kami Rita Sherpa's own peers — absorbs the mountain's fatal risk in direct support of paying clients.

story.title: 2015: The Mountain Shakes Base Camp Itself
story.narration: A magnitude-7.8 earthquake on 25 April 2015 triggers an avalanche that strikes South Base Camp directly, killing at least 19 people — the single deadliest day in Everest's history. The season is closed to summit attempts, and the disaster proves that even Base Camp, long treated as a place of relative safety, sits inside the mountain's hazard zone.

story.title: 2019: The Queue in the Death Zone
story.narration: In May 2019, a photograph by Nirmal Purja showing roughly 200 climbers queued along a single fixed rope near the summit goes viral, crystallizing years of overcrowding concern. Eleven climbers die that season, several after prolonged exposure waiting in the death zone.

story.title: The World's Highest Garbage Dump
story.narration: Decades of abandoned oxygen canisters, tents, and human waste earn Everest the label "the world's highest garbage dump." Climate change compounds the problem: the warming Khumbu Glacier is melting and exposing previously buried waste and bodies while destabilizing the icefall above South Base Camp.

story.title: Regulating a Mountain That Won't Sit Still
story.narration: Nepal's Department of Tourism responds with a $4,000 refundable waste deposit per climber and periodic cleanup expeditions, but leaves the deeper driver — permit volume, routinely 300–400 per season — largely untouched.

story.title: An Elite Frontier Sold as a Guided Package
story.narration: Messner's unassisted 1978 ascent and Kami Rita Sherpa's 30-plus fixed-rope summits sit at opposite poles of what climbing Everest now means: an elite athletic frontier on one hand, a guided, oxygen-assisted package on the other. Nearly every modern controversy about who Everest is for runs through that unresolved tension.

insights.title: Everest's death-zone queuing turns a fixed-rope bottleneck into a fatality multiplier
insights.body: Above 8,000 m, every extra hour without supplemental oxygen sharply raises the risk of high-altitude cerebral and pulmonary edema. The 2019 photograph of roughly 200 climbers queued on a single rope made visible what had been building for years: narrow summit-day terrain cannot absorb rising permit volume without converting wait time directly into death-zone mortality risk.

insights.title: Sherpa guides absorb a disproportionate share of Everest's fatal risk while remaining structurally invisible in summit narratives
insights.body: The Icefall Doctors fix the route through the Khumbu Icefall; Sherpa porters and guides cross it repeatedly to ferry supplies for clients who cross it once or twice. The 2014 avalanche, which killed sixteen Nepali guides and porters, made explicit a pattern that summit-count narratives (including Kami Rita Sherpa's own record) tend to obscure: occupational risk on Everest is not evenly distributed between clients and the Sherpa workforce that supports them.

insights.title: The 1996 disaster failed to slow commercial guiding growth — permit volume kept rising for decades after eight deaths in a day
insights.body: Rob Hall and Scott Fischer's deaths, and the wide readership of "Into Thin Air," made 1996 the most publicized cautionary tale in Everest's history. Yet Nepal's permit issuance expanded rather than contracted in the following decades, routinely exceeding 300–400 per season by the late 2010s — the opposite of what the disaster's warning would predict.

insights.title: Climate-driven glacier melt is simultaneously destabilizing the Khumbu Icefall and exhuming decades of buried expedition waste
insights.body: Warming temperatures act on the same glacier in two directions at once: they destabilize the ice structures of the Khumbu Icefall, a hazard climbers must cross regardless, and they melt back the ice that had been quietly burying oxygen canisters, tents, and bodies for decades, converting a hidden waste problem into a visible one.

insights.title: Nepal's $4,000 waste-deposit rule shifts cleanup incentives onto individual climbers but leaves permit volume — the deeper driver of crowding — unregulated
insights.body: The waste deposit is a targeted, climber-level fix for a visible symptom (trash on the mountain). It does nothing to address the root cause repeatedly implicated in 1996, 2019, and the general death-zone queuing pattern: the number of permits Nepal's Department of Tourism issues each season.

insights.title: Messner and Habeler's unassisted 1978 summit and today's oxygen-assisted guided ascents represent two incompatible definitions of what climbing Everest means
insights.body: One tradition treats Everest as the outer limit of unassisted human physiology; the other treats it as a fixed-rope, oxygen-supported package sold to clients with widely varying experience. Both traditions use the same mountain, the same base camps, and often the same season — and the tension between them underlies most current debate about how Everest should be regulated.

clusters.label: Geography & Camps
clusters.description: The two base camps, the routes and hazards above them, and the national territories that administer access to each side of the mountain.

clusters.label: First Ascent Era
clusters.description: The people and events that established Everest as a climbable, then conquered, objective — from Mallory and Irvine's unresolved 1924 disappearance to Hillary and Norgay's confirmed 1953 summit.

clusters.label: Extreme Performance
clusters.description: The athletic frontier tradition of climbing Everest at the limit of unassisted human physiology.

clusters.label: Commercial Guiding & the 1996 Disaster
clusters.description: The rise of commercial guiding companies and the storm that turned their business model into a cautionary tale.

clusters.label: Sherpa Labor & Safety
clusters.description: The Sherpa workforce that operates the Nepali side of the mountain, and the disasters that most starkly exposed the risk they carry.

clusters.label: Crowding, Waste & Regulation
clusters.description: The modern crisis cluster: rising climber volume, the waste it leaves behind, and Nepal's limited regulatory response to both.

nodes.label: Mount Everest
nodes.description: The highest mountain above sea level on Earth, straddling the Nepal–China border in the Mahalangur Himal; the summit objective every route and camp in this report ultimately serves.

nodes.label: South Base Camp
nodes.description: The Nepali staging camp at roughly 5,364 m on the Khumbu Glacier, reached by trek from Lukla; the busier, more commercialized of the two base camps and the launch point for the South Col route.

nodes.label: North Base Camp
nodes.description: The Tibetan staging camp at roughly 5,150 m near Rongbuk Monastery, reachable by vehicle; launch point for the North Ridge route, administered under Chinese permitting.

nodes.label: Khumbu Icefall
nodes.description: A constantly shifting field of house-sized ice seracs and crevasses directly above South Base Camp, crossed dozens of times per expedition on fixed ladders maintained by the Icefall Doctors.

nodes.label: Khumbu Glacier
nodes.description: The glacier underlying South Base Camp and feeding the Khumbu Icefall; warming temperatures are melting it, destabilizing the icefall and exposing decades of buried expedition waste.

nodes.label: The Death Zone
nodes.description: The region above 8,000 m where atmospheric oxygen is roughly a third of sea-level pressure and the human body cannot acclimatize, only deteriorate; the setting for nearly every fatal Everest incident.

nodes.label: The Second Step
nodes.description: A near-vertical rock band above 8,600 m on the North Ridge route, long the route's defining technical obstacle until a fixed ladder made it passable for commercial climbers.

nodes.label: South Col Route
nodes.description: The standard climbing route from South Base Camp through the Khumbu Icefall and South Col to the summit; the route of the 1953 first ascent.

nodes.label: North Ridge Route
nodes.description: The standard climbing route from North Base Camp over the North Ridge, past the Second Step, to the summit.

nodes.label: Rongbuk Monastery
nodes.description: A Tibetan monastery near North Base Camp that marks the traditional starting point of the North Side approach.

nodes.label: Lukla
nodes.description: The Nepali town whose airstrip is the starting point of the multi-day trek to South Base Camp.

nodes.label: Namche Bazaar
nodes.description: The principal Sherpa trading town on the trek route between Lukla and South Base Camp.

nodes.label: Nepal
nodes.description: The country administering the South Side of Everest, including South Base Camp, the Sagarmatha Zone, and the climbing permit system.

nodes.label: Tibet Autonomous Region
nodes.description: The Chinese administrative region on Everest's north side, controlling access to North Base Camp and the North Ridge route.

nodes.label: Edmund Hillary
nodes.description: New Zealand mountaineer who, with Tenzing Norgay, made the first confirmed summit of Everest in 1953.

nodes.label: Tenzing Norgay
nodes.description: Nepali Sherpa climber who, with Edmund Hillary, made the first confirmed summit of Everest in 1953; his ascent anchors the Sherpa community's mountaineering legacy.

nodes.label: John Hunt
nodes.description: British expedition leader who organized and led the 1953 expedition that put Hillary and Norgay on the summit.

nodes.label: 1953 First Ascent
nodes.description: The first confirmed ascent of Everest, on 29 May 1953, via the South Col route — the foundational event of Everest mountaineering.

nodes.label: George Mallory
nodes.description: British mountaineer who disappeared with Andrew Irvine high on the North Ridge in 1924; whether he reached the summit before dying remains unresolved.

nodes.label: Andrew Irvine
nodes.description: British mountaineer who disappeared with George Mallory on the North Ridge in 1924; his body has never been located.

nodes.label: 1924 Mallory & Irvine Disappearance
nodes.description: The 1924 disappearance of Mallory and Irvine high on the North Ridge, leaving open the question of whether they summited 29 years before Hillary and Norgay's confirmed ascent.

nodes.label: 1999 Discovery of Mallory's Body
nodes.description: The 1999 discovery of George Mallory's body on Everest, which narrowed but did not resolve the mystery of the 1924 disappearance.

nodes.label: Reinhold Messner
nodes.description: Italian mountaineer who, with Peter Habeler, made the first ascent of Everest without supplemental oxygen in 1978, redefining the limits of unassisted high-altitude performance.

nodes.label: Peter Habeler
nodes.description: Austrian mountaineer who, with Reinhold Messner, made the first ascent of Everest without supplemental oxygen in 1978.

nodes.label: 1978 No-Oxygen Ascent
nodes.description: The 1978 first ascent of Everest without supplemental oxygen by Messner and Habeler, disproving the era's assumption that the summit was physiologically impossible unassisted.

nodes.label: Rob Hall
nodes.description: New Zealand mountain guide, founder of Adventure Consultants, who died on Everest during the 1996 disaster.

nodes.label: Scott Fischer
nodes.description: American mountain guide, founder of Mountain Madness, who died on Everest during the 1996 disaster.

nodes.label: 1996 Everest Disaster
nodes.description: A rogue storm caught multiple guided groups near the summit on 10–11 May 1996, killing eight climbers in a single day — the defining cautionary narrative about commercial climbing volume and compressed summit windows.

nodes.label: Jon Krakauer
nodes.description: American journalist and client-climber who survived the 1996 disaster and chronicled it in "Into Thin Air."

nodes.label: Into Thin Air
nodes.description: Jon Krakauer's account of the 1996 Everest disaster, which became the defining cautionary narrative about commercial high-altitude guiding.

nodes.label: Adventure Consultants
nodes.description: Commercial guiding company founded by Rob Hall, central to the 1996 Everest disaster.

nodes.label: Mountain Madness
nodes.description: Commercial guiding company founded by Scott Fischer, central to the 1996 Everest disaster.

nodes.label: Icefall Doctors
nodes.description: A dedicated Sherpa team that fixes ropes and ladders through the Khumbu Icefall each season, maintaining the passage every South Side expedition depends on.

nodes.label: Kami Rita Sherpa
nodes.description: Nepali Sherpa mountaineer who holds the record for most Everest summits by any individual, having passed 30 by the mid-2020s.

nodes.label: 2014 Khumbu Icefall Avalanche
nodes.description: An avalanche in the Khumbu Icefall on 18 April 2014 killed sixteen Nepali guides and porters, triggering a labor action that shut down that season's climbing.

nodes.label: 2015 Earthquake Avalanche
nodes.description: The magnitude-7.8 Nepal earthquake of 25 April 2015 triggered an avalanche that struck South Base Camp directly, killing at least 19 people — the deadliest single day in Everest's history.

nodes.label: Nirmal Purja
nodes.description: Nepali mountaineer who photographed the viral 2019 image of roughly 200 climbers queued on a single fixed rope near the summit.

nodes.label: 2019 Summit Traffic Jam
nodes.description: A May 2019 photograph of a roughly 200-climber queue near the summit went viral, crystallizing years of overcrowding concern; eleven climbers died that season, several attributed to prolonged death-zone exposure while queuing.

nodes.label: Overcrowding Crisis
nodes.description: The buildup of climber volume on narrow summit-day terrain, driven by rising permit issuance and commercial guiding growth, that produces death-zone queuing and elevated fatality risk.

nodes.label: "World's Highest Garbage Dump" Crisis
nodes.description: Decades of abandoned oxygen canisters, tents, ropes, and human waste on Everest's upper camps, earning the mountain the informal label "the world's highest garbage dump."

nodes.label: Nepal Department of Tourism
nodes.description: The Nepali government agency that issues South Side climbing permits and administers waste-deposit and cleanup requirements, generating significant revenue but facing criticism for not capping climber volume.

nodes.label: Waste Deposit Regulation
nodes.description: Nepal's requirement that each climber post a $4,000 waste deposit, refunded only if a minimum weight of trash is brought back — a mechanism aimed at the waste crisis that leaves permit volume itself unregulated.

nodes.label: Sherpa Community
nodes.description: The Sherpa people of the Khumbu region who form the operational backbone of South Side climbing — porters, Icefall Doctors, and guides — while bearing a disproportionate share of the mountain's fatal risk.
